: some of the notes are in his hand and may have obtained other items from his father, William Jenney (d. 1483), who was administered to Lincoln's Inn in 1430, and was Justice of the King's Bench 1481-1483. The issues of William Jenney, the eldest son of Edmund, and Francis Jenney (b. 1510) , son of William, on ff. 8r-9v suggest that the manuscript passed down to his son and grandson. Preliminary note:Much of the medieval and early modern provenance of MS Dd.4.24 remains uncertain. The manuscript contains numerous annotations and inscriptions, often of names - all, some or none of which may be connected with its ownership. Many of the connections between these names and specific individuals were first put forward by John Manly and Edith Rickert (1940), but the evidence is often tenuous and the connections speculative, and they remain the subject of some debate. See Seymour (1997), Mosser (2011) and Da Rold (2013) for further discussion. Rather than reproduce what was proposed by Manly and Rickert, this description will instead list the locations and approximate dates of the names written into MS Dd.4.24, providing convenient links to these instances and the basis for future research.

overview: history: Ian Harwood identified Mathew Holmes as the copyist of CUL MS Dd.5.78.3 and three other lute books in 1963. It has been possible to place Holmes' books in chronological order and Dd.5.78.3 is the second. It may have been started at Oxford where Holmes was precentor and singingman at Christ Church between 1588 and 1597 but was probably largely compiled after 1597 when Holmes moved to become 'chanter' and singingman at Westminster Abbey. It is not known when or where the manuscript was handled by John Dowland who added a title to his piece, Farwelland his name on fol. 44r.It seems likely that all Holmes' manuscripts were together in Westminster at the time of his death in 1621. It is not known when or by what means they entered the University Library. The first reference to Dd.5.78.3 is in CUL MS Oo.7.53, a manuscript catalogue of the library compiled in 1753.

Folios i-iv written and owned by of the Diocese of York and Principal of Beef Hall in Oxford, c. 1496-1497. Popley may also have owned ff. Edmund Popley Popley, Edmund 1r-77v, which would explain how his notes came to be bound with the rest of the volume, but there is no strong evidence to rule for or against Popley's ownership of ff. 1r-77v. The first four medieval endleaves in the volume (ff. i-iv) are in Popley's hand and contain a copy of the Articuli Cleri enacted in 1316 (ff. ii recto - iv verso), followed by some brief legal notes (f. iv verso). Popley signed the notes on f. iv verso as 'Edmundus Poplay' and mentioned a connection to an unspecified university ('studia quindecim annorum que habuit in hac uniuersitate in facultate arcium') and recorded the date of a legal action as 12 June 1489 ('Hec gracia concessa et confirmata est anno domini millesimo cccco lxxxxix mensia Jun. xiimo'). The name, the date, and the long connection to a university allows for the Poplay of ff. i-iv to be identified as the Edmund Poplay (Popley) of the Diocese of York, who was ordained as a deacon in 1484 and was Principal of Beef Hall in Oxford c. 1496-1497. There is no codicological evidence for or against the union of Parts 1 (ff. i-iv) and 2 (ff. 1r-77v) in 1489 , so it is not possible to determine if Poplay was the owner of ff. 1r-77v, or if their composite arrangement occured later, but Poplay's ownership of ff. 1r-77v offers the simplest explanation for how his notes came to be with the main section of MS 412. On fol. 56v, Edward Pierce is described as >Regie Capellae, suggesting that this piece was written in or before 1600 when Pierce left the Chapel Royal to go to St Paul's.Harwood (2010) suggests that Holmes took his books to Westminster Abbey in 1597 when he became 'chanter' and singingman. This document was used as the binding for CUL MS Nn.6.36, a lute book. Ian Harwood identified Mathew Holmes as the copyist of CUL MS Dd.9.33 and three other lute books in 1963. It has been possible to place Holmes' books in chronological order and Dd.9.33 is the third. It was copied at Westminster where Holmes was chanter and singingman from 1597 until his death in 1621. Harwood (1963:46-47) suggests that the two requests for prayers for the sick men Davie Were [Wier] and William Hoper [Hooper] which Holmes wrote on the back flyleaf of the manuscript may have been rough drafts for memoranda collected by Holmes as part of his duties within the Abbey. Thieving Lane, where Davie lived, was in the parish of St Margaret's, Westminster and most of its houses belonged to the Abbey. The parish register records the burial of Davie Wier on 18 March 1600. The Westminster parish register records the burial of William Hooper on 15 April 1601.It seems likely that all the manuscripts copied by Holmes were together in Westminster at the time of his death in 1621, although some were copied in Oxford before his move to Westminster. Cambridge, Fitzwilliam Museum, MS McClean 89 (hereafter MS McClean 89) is a Book of Hours made in Flanders in the late 15th century for the English book market. The manuscript was in England by 1515 at the latest, since several generations of the Skipwith family of South Ormsby in Lincolnshire added birth records to the calendar (ff. 27r-32v) and to some of the endleaves (ff. 128r-129v). The Skipwith family were minor gentry, and several members of the family were involved in local and national politics and also married into socially powerful families. The birth records in MS McClean 89 are worth close examination, not only as a primary source of new biographical information about several socially and politically important figures in England in the 16th and 17th centuries, but also because the records allow us to trace the transfer of the volume from one generation to another through four generations of the Skipwith family. In addition, the birth records are especially important as a way to highlight the family of Lyon (also known as Leo, Lionel) Skipwith, eldest son of the marriage between Sir William Skipwith and Alice Dymoke, whose children seem to have been erroneously attributed to his younger brother Henry Skipwith in many accounts of the family history (more information below). The first member of the Skipwith family to use MS McClean 89 was , High Sheriff of Lincolnshire 1526-1527, MP for Lincolnshire in 1529 and 1539 (see Sir William Skipwith (b. ?1488, d. 1547) Sir William Skipwith, b. ?1488, d. 1547 History of Parliament entry for further details), and son of Sir John Skipwith (d. ?1518), High Sheriff of Lincolnshire 1493 and Katherine Skipwith (née Fitzwilliam). Sir William was married twice, first to Elizabeth Tyrwhitt, by whom he had one son, also named William (born c. 1510) (for whom also see History of Parliament entry) before Elizabeth's death in or before the year 1514. Sir William then married Alice Dymoke, daughter of Sir Lionel Dymoke; the date is not recorded, but the marriage probably took place in or before mid-1514, since William recorded the births of his children with Alice Dymoke in MS McClean 89, beginning with Marie (Mary), who was born 15 March 1515. Records in a number of hands record the births of a further twelve of his children in the manuscript's calendar pages, summarised as follows in chronological order (for full transcriptions and interpretations, see Additions): Marie (Mary), born 15 March 1515 Jane, born 26 October 1516 Lyon (also known as Leo and Lionel), born 3 December 1517 Anna, born 30 March 1518 John and Margaret, born 11 June 1519 Brigida (Bridget), born 2 February 1521 Katryn (Katheryn, Katherine), born 6 December 1523 Elisabeth (Elizabeth), born 20 January 1524 George, born 12 December 1526 Dorothea, born 6 February 1527 George, born 30 November 1529 Henry, born 1 September 1532 There are a number of unresolved complexities in this list of births. In three instances, it appears that births occur too close together for Alice Dymoke to be the mother of both children: Lyon on 3 December 1517 and Anna on 30 March 1518; Katryn on 6 December 1523 and Elisabeth on 20 January 1524; and George on 12 December 1526 and Dorothea on 6 February 1527. The manner in which the dates are recorded in the manuscript varies: by regnal years, calendar years, or some combination thereof. There were also at this time differing practices in reckoning the start of the year: the calendar/Christian year began on 1 January, but the legal year on 25 March. The impossibly short gap between the births of Katryn and Elisabeth, and between George and Dorothea, might be explained by confusion arising from these different systems, if Katryn were born on 6 December 1522 not 1523, and if George were born on 6 February 1528, not 1527. However, no such resolution is possible for Lyon and Anna, since their birth dates are too closely pre- and post-dated by their siblings Jane and twins John and Margaret. One possibility is that some of these children were born out of wedlock to another mother, though the naming of Lyon (presumably in honour of his maternal grandfather) and the descent of the manuscript to him suggests that he was legitimate (further details below). A further question hangs over the two children named George: perhaps the first died in infancy. Further research is needed to place all of these observations on firmer evidential ground. It is notable that the birth of Sir William's first child (William, b. ?1510), by his first wife Elizabeth, is not recorded here. Furthermore, the book passed not to this William, but to the oldest son, Lyon (b. 1517), of Sir William's second marriage to Alice. This suggests the possibility that MS McClean 89 came into the Skipwith family via Alice herself, and who wished it to remain in her side of the family. Lyon was married twice, first to Margaret Barnardiston, daughter of John Barnardiston, and second to Jane Bracebridge, daughter of William Bracebridge. The births of seven of his children were recorded in MS McClean 89, all in the same hand, which might indicate that Lyon added the entries himself. The children of Lyon Skipwith as recorded in MS McClean 89 are as follows: Katheryne (Katherine), born 10 July 1555 Margaret, born 8 March 1561 (or 1562) Elizabeth, born 15 February 1562 Ursula, born 30 May 1563 William, born 12 September 1566 George, born 4 November 1567 John, born 9 March 1573 Lyon Skipwith has not left a substantial trace in the historical record, and as a result some sources appear to conflate details of his life with those of his youngest brother, Henry (b. 1 September 1532). For instance, in Burke's Peerage, Knightage and Baronetage ((2003), III.3641), Henry is said to have had twelve children (William, Francis, Henry, George, Ursula, Catherine, Anne, Jane, Bridget, Dorothy, Elizabeth, Margaret), but the records added to MS McClean 89 indicate that some of these are Lyon's children. Further suggestive evidence is provided by the descent of the manuscript, which passed to William (b. 1566), since it is more likely that he inherited it as Lyon's son, rather than as his nephew. was Sheriff of Leicestershire c. 1598, and MP for Leicestershire in 1601 and for Leicester in 1604 (see William Skipwith (b. 1566, d. 1610) William Skipwith, 1566-1610 History of Parliament entry). He was knighted in 1603 and was married twice, first to Margaret Cave and second to Jane Roberts, the daughter of John Roberts of Wollaston. Like his antecedents, he recorded the births of six children on ff. 128r-128v, as follows: Jane, born 3 November 1587 Anne, born 23 January 1588 Henry, born 21 March 1590 George, born 12 February 1591 Elizabeth, born 11 February 1592 Thomas, born 6 August 1594 MS McClean 89 passed to William's eldest male child, . Henry was knighted in 1609 and was married twice, first to Anne Kempe, daughter of Sir Thomas Kempe and second to Blandina Pennen, daughter of John Pennen of Badgeworth, Somerset. He too recorded the births of seven children on ff. Henry Skipwith (b. 1590) Henry Skipwith, b. 1590 129r-129v, as follows: William, born 25 February 1613 Henry, born 16 December 1615 Elizabeth, born 6 October 1617 Thomas, born 30 March 1618 Diana, born 27 May 1621 Graye, born 23 January 1622 Anne, born 23 February 1623 There are no further Skipwith births recorded in MS McClean 89 after this last entry, and the subsequent ownership of the manuscript is unknown.

German, made for, or at, the Benedictine nunnery of Holzen, Allmannshofen, founded in 1153. The MS. was acquired by Archbishop William Laud (d. 1645) in Germany between 1636 and 1638. Laud was a major collector of manuscripts. At the foot of f.1 “Liber Collegii S. Petri in academia Cantabrigiensi ex dono Iohannis Rothwell ciuis et stationarii Londinensis. Ita testor, Lazarus Seaman Magister”. Lazarus Seaman (d. 1675), was admitted Master of Peterhouse, Cambridge, by Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Manchester, in place of John Cosin, on 11 April 1644 and remained so until 1660. With this note, he testified that the MS. had been donated by the London bookseller John Rothwell - probably the elder John Rothwell, who was active at the Sun in St Paul’s churchyard from 1628 to 1649, rather than his son, also John, who inherited the business.

The manuscript is a composite and is comprised of nine distinct Parts. Two of the Parts (Parts 4 and 9) have inscriptions demonstrating that they were the property of members of the community of in Cumbria by the middle of the Lanercost PrioryLanercost Priory (Gilsland, England)14th century, and it possible that all Parts of Peterhouse MS 247 were copied or at least compiled at Lanercost Priory. Part 4 (ff. 79-155, see f. 79r) has an inscription on its first leaf describing it as the property of the community of Lanercost Priory ('Liber Sancte Marie magdalene de Lanrecost Si quis inde eum asportauerit anathema sit'), and Part 9 (f. 175, see f. 175r) has an inscription describing the gift of the book (in whatever form it was in then) as the possession of a particular monk, Nicholas of Morland, during John of Bewcastle's tenure as Prior (1338-1354). Please see the provenance information for Parts 4 and 9 and Pam Robinson's introduction to this catalogue record for further information. Several Parts of the manuscript share similar scribal and decorative features so it is possible that the entire volume existed in its current form at Lanercost in the 14th century. This manuscript (or, at least, some of its Parts) is one of only three surviving manuscripts known to have been owned and used at Lanercost Priory, the others being and London, British Library, MS Cotton Claudius D vii ('The Lanercost Chronicle') . overview: history: Newnham College MS 4 was probably commissioned by an owner whose heraldic badge or rebus has been drawn no less than four times in the manuscript's lower margins (ff. 1r, 35r, 68v, and 98v). This badge/rebus consists of an eagle displayed with a Lombard letter 'L' in red ink on its chest and standing on a green mound. If it is a heraldic badge, then it is not recorded in Michael Powell Siddons. If it is a rebus, which seems more likely, then the eagle probably refers to the first name 'John' or surname 'St John'. Reading the rebus as 'L over St John', a possible solution is 'Oliver St John'. Considering the manuscript's dating, he could have been Sir Oliver St John of Bletsoe, Bedfordshire; Spelsbury, Oxfordshire; and Lydiard Tregoze, Wiltshire (d. 1437), the great-great-great grandfather of Oliver St John, 1st Baron St John of Bletso (d. 1582). His ownership of a Heraldic badges in England and Wales (Woodbridge: Boydell, 2009)Piers Plowman manuscript would fit with what else is known about book ownership by the St Johns of Bletsoe. The family owned a Middle English translation of the Legenda Aurea, known as the Gilte Legende, dating to the 2nd or 3rd quarter of the 15th century () and perhaps also a printed copy of William Caxton's London, British Library, Harley MS 4775Dictes and Sayings of the Philosophers (London, 1477) [STC 6828]). Another possible solution is 'John Elred' - reading the rebus as 'John red L' - in which case the commissioner may have been John Elvered, also spelled 'Elred', who occurs as rector of Oxburgh, Norfolk, in 1386. Elred held this position until 1416 when his will was drawn up on 1 October and proved on the 16th of that month. According to the London, British Library, C. 10 b. 2, p. 132, 'John Elred' used a seal with an image of St Michael slaying the dragon at its centre, a coat of arms with St Clare on his its right side, and a coat of arms with an eagle displayed on its left side (for a reproduction, see Dictionary of British Arms, vol. 2 (London: Society of Antiquaries, 1996)). Sigilla Antiqua: Engravings from ancient seals attached to deeds and charters in the Muniment room of Sir Thomas Hare, baronet of Stowe-Bardolph, 2nd series (1862), no. 3.8.

overview: history: The name 'Will(?elmus) Walter(?us)' on f. 86r next to a Latin couplet (see Contents for further information) and the word 'llinpenff'(?), all in what appears to be the same 16th-century hand. A William Walter (d. 1523) was known to Henry VII, whom he briefly served as an envoy at the papal curia in the late 1490s. This Walter had studied at Bologna earlier in that decade and was subsequently recorded as doctor of canon and civil law there; he spent the last two decades of his life as archdeacon of Brecon. The word 'llinpenff' bears the hallmarks of an as yet unidentified Welsh placename that began 'Llyn...' (meaning 'lake'), which is also suggestive of a possible connection between this manuscript and this Walter. Another William Walter (fl. c. 1525-1533), poet and translator, was alive around this time. He may have been the owner of , a copy of the Canterbury Tales, which bears an ownership inscription matching his name, written in a later, different style of handwriting to the inscription found in MS Ii.5.11. Little is known about this second Walter's life, and Ralph Griffiths has put forward suggestive evidence that the two Walters are one and the same. London, British Library, MS Sloane 1686, f. 1r R. Griffiths, ' From Bologna to Brecon: The Cosmopolitan World of a Pre-Reformation Archdeacon', Medieval Prosopography 33 (2018), pp. 153-166A.S.G. Edwards, 'Walter, William (fl. c. 1525-1533), Oxford Dictionary of National Biography (2004) [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/28641]

Probably owned by , Alice de Reydon Reydon, Alice denée Reymes, wife of Robert de Reydon. Her obituary is added to the Calendar in a contemporary hand, on the 5th July (fol. 16r): 'Obitus Alicie de Reidon anno domini Mo ccco x...'. The year is uncertain, but must be after 1310 (the first limb of 'x' is visible; if any number followed, it has been cropped) but before 1323: the Inquisitions Post Mortem held in that year on Alice's husband gives the name of his widow as Margaret. The manuscript may have been produced for her prior to her marriage, since her family's coat of arms features on f. 19r. The female figures on ff. 1v and 19r may have been intended to represent her: the mantle of the former figure has had the Reymes family coat of arms painted over it (the cross or has been divided in two vertically and painted along each edge). Cirencester AbbeyCirencester, Augustinian abbey of St Mary the Virgin5) and the Geoffrey of Monmouth quire (ff. 213–222) are of an undetermined English origin. Both these and the verse anthology (ff. 223–237) appear to be additions, since Sol meldunensis has a planned conclusion at f. 212v, though not copied with the earlier part of the page; and the additions have a reduced level of annotation in comparison to ff. 3–212. A consistent decoration scheme found across the manuscript (added to Geoffrey of Monmouth at f. 214r) show that all parts of the volume were at one point at Cirencester. A possible interpretation of this evidence is that on receipt of the manuscript, the monks of Malmesbury added marginal additions, the friars miniature, and Geoffrey of Monmouth before returning the manuscript to the canons of Cirencester, who integrated the additions through decoration and appended the verse anthology before sending the book back to Malmesbury.

Carew is principally known for the collection of books on Irish history that he amassed as an administrator in Ireland between 1574 and 1592. He bequeathed this collection to Sir Thomas Stafford (d. 1655), from whom they passed to William Laud (1573–1645), Archbishop of Canterbury. The latter placed forty-two volumes at Lambeth Library while four reached the Bodleian Library as part of the Laudian collection [see M.R. About Carew's possession of medieval manuscripts from England much less is known, but these appear to have travelled different routes after they left his collection. A John Brampton held a tenement near Bishopsgate from the Hospital of St Bartholomew and was auditor of the accounts of the Wardens of London Bridget in arrear in 1467. The latter was MP for London in 1472-5, collector of the Petty Custom until 1483, and royal pensioner in 1485-6. One of the manuscripts of , Baron Carew of Clopton and Earl of Totnes: his signature (George Carew (1555-1629) Carew, George, 1555-1629G: Carew) inscribed in dark ink at the top of f. 1:3v. Carew is principally known for the collection of books on Irish history that he amassed as an administrator in Ireland between 1574 and 1592. He bequeathed this collection to Sir Thomas Stafford (d. 1655), from whom they passed to William Laud (1573–1645), Archbishop of Canterbury. The latter placed forty-two volumes at Lambeth Library while four reached the Bodleian Library as part of the Laudian collection (see M.R. James, 'The Carew Manuscripts', ; The English Historical Review, 42 (1927), 261-267James H. Todd, 'Account of an Ancient Irish Manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, Oxford', ; and Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, 2 (1936-1869), 336-346Ute Lotz-Heumann, 'Carew, George, earl of Totnes (1555–1629)', ). About Carew's possession of medieval manuscripts from England much less is known, but these appear to have travelled different routes after they left his collection. His signature ( (2004) [accessed 23 February 2024]Oxford Dictionary of National BiographyG: Carew) can be found in at least six such medieval manuscripts (besides the present volume): (f. 1v) (James, III, p. 115)Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.22 (f. 1:1r) (James, III, pp. 361-62)Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.7.23 (f. 1r) [identified in the online record: 'MS 107: Composite manuscript including twenty-four texts, 13th-14th century']Edinburgh, University Library, MS 107 (f. 1r)London, British Library, Harley MS 204 (f. 7r)London, British library, Harley MS 223 (f. 1r) (see London, British Library, Harley MS 234Andrew G. Watson, ; The Library of Sir Simonds D'Ewes (London: British Museum, 1966), pp. 210-211 (no. 926)Cyril Ernest Wright, )Fontes Harleiani: A Study of the Sources of the Harleian Collection of Manuscripts Preserved in the Department of Manuscripts in the British Museum (London: British Museum, 1972), p. 96 It is possible that Carew received all these manuscripts from John Dee. A note on f. i verso, badly rubbed: 'Caucio Walteri de Wasten exponitur ciste Batulfi ... concepionis beate Marie anno Domini Mo CCCo xxx', i.e., the book was pledged as surety for a loan and placed in Botolph's chest on 8 December 1330 by Walter de Wasten. Caucio inscriptions in manuscripts reflect a practice common (but not limited) to Oxford and Cambridge in the 14th and 15th centuries where borrowers could pledge books or other high-value items in exchange for a monetary loan supplied by a lender who would store the manuscript in a chest for the duration of the loan. The loan chests and their funds were often supplied by a single benefactor whose name became associated with the chest long after their death and became incorporated into the Caucio inscriptions usually in the form 'ciste [name]'; in this case, the 'ciste Batulfi' probably refers to a loan-chest in Cambridge known as 'Botoloph's Chest', which, if that identification is correct, places at least some parts of Peterhouse MS 251 in Cambridge in December 1330. 'Botolph's Chest' was supposedly endowed by a Thomas de St Botolph, chaplain to John Le Romeyn, archbishop of York, see Fuller and Billingfield, 'Section IV' in The History of the University of Cambridge, esp. p. 130. This Caucio note is briefly discussed in Thomson's Catalogue, p. 158; Thomson suggests that 'Walteri de Wasten' may be the Walter de Weston in Emden BRUC, p. 631, a cleric of Cambridge who complained about the violence from the mayor and townspeople of Cambridge in 1322 as recorded in Calendar of the Patent Rolls preserved in the Public Record Office 1216-1509, 54 vols (1891-1916). The Caucio note is also briefly discussed in CBMLC 10 UC48.291 where the note is transcribed as follows: 'Caucio Walter de Kasten exspositus ciste Botulph' Concepionis beate Marie anno Domini Mo ccco xxx' T. The precise date of acquisition is unknown, but the manuscript was certainly at Peterhouse by 1418 as it is recorded in the 1418 inventory of the Peterhouse library. The early 15th-century inventory of the library is preserved in a document now known as the Registrum vetus ('The Old Register'). The Registrum vetus was begun in 1418 by a single scribe, and subsequent donations to the library were added by other members of the College throughout the 15th century. The reference to Peterhouse MS 178 occurs on p. 17 of the Registrum vetus where it is recorded as part of the original inventory of 1418 by the main scribe of the Registrum. The entry in the Registrum vetus for MS 178 is as follows: 'Liber magistri Ricardi experti in qualibet parte medicine --- Incipit in 2. The manuscript has retained the codicological form it had in 1418 as the secundo folio (f. o fo lapis in penultimo de albedine2r) and penultimate leaf (f. 310r keywords match those in the extant manuscript 'lapis' and 'de albedine' respectively. overview: history: Another Part (pp. 111-446) or perhaps the extant entirety of this manuscript may once have belonged to and may have been donated by him to his former College, Peterhouse in Cambridge. For her article on Roger Marchall's ownership and use of manuscripts Linda Voigts examined the Roger Marchall (c. 1417-1477) Rogerus Marshall (c. 1417-1477) Registrum Vetus of Peterhouse, which includes an added slip (now p. 22 of that book) in Marchall's hand and which records a list of twelve manuscript donations to the College ('Billa magistri Rogeri Marshall de dono suo scripta propria manu sua anno domini 1472' / 'Magister Roger Marchall's list of his donation written by his own hand in the year of the Lord 1472'); Marchall describes the 8th item on the list as the 'Cirurgia lamfranci'. Voigts then notes that this volume, i.e., Gonville and Caius MS 159/209 'contains Cirurgia Lanfranci as text 3, a physically separable section (pp. 111-443 of a 445-page manuscript) with RM title.' It is possible then that either what is now Gonville and Caius MS 159/209 pp. 111-446 or what is now Gonville and Caius MS 159/209 in its entirety is the same item referred to in Marchall's 1472 list of manuscripts for donation to the Peterhouse library. There is no clear record of when or by what means MS 159/209 entered the library collection of Gonville and Caius, but the present manuscript is one of eighteen (possibly nineteen) manuscripts at Gonville and Caius College that may be linked to Marchall, the others of which were probably donated by him to Gonville Hall (as Gonville and Caius then was) before his death. See L. Voigts, 'A doctor and his books: the manuscripts of Roger Marchall (d. 1477)', in R. Beadle and A. J. The text of the Emendatio uitae by in this manuscript, ff. Richard Rolle Rolle, Richard, 1290?-1349 74r-99v is, according to Rüdiger Spahl, a direct copy of the same text in , a 14th century copy of the text. According to Spahl, MS Harley 5235 must have served as the direct exemplar for MS Jesus Q.D.4 as the two manuscripts contain fourteen shared textual omissions not found in any other copies of the text, and corrections made by the Harley scribe to the text of the London, British Library, MS Harley 5235, ff. 1r-11v Emendatio uitae after the main copying stint had been completed are also found in MS Q.D.4. Spahl supplies other evidence for the archetype-child relationship between these two manuscripts and positions both within his 'zeta' subgroup. London, British Library, MS Harley 5235 is a composite manuscript, and the Part with the Emendatio uitae was apparently copied in the late-14th or early-15th century. Harley MS 5235 does not have a complete provenance, and its earliest known owner is a 'Thomas Baylle' who seems to have owned the manuscript in the 16th century, which is too late to provide any information about the origins of Jesus College MS Q.D.4. Acquired by Jesus College before c. 1700, but the precise date and the circumstances of the acquisition are unknown. Jesus College MS Q.B.10 is not one of the seven books at Jesus College described in the Ecloga of Thomas James (1600), nor is it included in Bernard's Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (c. 1697), although the lack of inclusion in Bernard does not preclude its arrival at Jesus College before 1697. Bernard's Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ reprinted James's Ecloga and occasionally updated the information therein, but unfortunately it is not a reliable guide to the 17th-century manuscript acquisitions of Jesus College, since it does not, for example, record the substantial donation of manuscripts to Jesus College by Thomas Man that is known to have taken place in 1685. Thomas Man donated a substantial portion of the medieval manuscripts that now belong to Jesus College as a gift to the Library in 1685, but MS Q.B.10 is almost certainly not a Man donation as MS Q.B.10 once had the Jesus College shelfmark 'M.Z.11'; and the Man donations were in all cases (apart from two that lack shelfmarks in that system entirely) assigned 'M.H.xx' numbers rather than 'M.Z.xx' numbers. The combination of former shelfmarks written in the volume, i.e., 'M.Z.11', 'H.18' 'N.B.10' and latterly 'Q.B.10' indicates that MS Q.B.10 was certainly present at Jesus College c. 1700, as c. 1700-1705 the manuscripts in the library were assigned new shelfmarks and MS Q.B.10 bears an 'M.Z.11' shelfmark which was in use before the reorganisation of the library c. 1700-1705. There is a Jesus College ownership inscription 'Liber Collegii Jesu' in ink on f. 2r in a late ?17th century or early ?18th century hand. See R. Hanna for a discussion of the reorganisation of the Jesus College Library c. 1700-1705 and the former shelfmark systems in use there: R. overview: history: When and how Peterhouse MS 95 came into the possession of the College library is not entirely clear; the volume probably passed into the College library collection in the 1470s (before 1477) through a donation by . Marchall was a doctor and manuscript collector, and was a royal physician to Edward IV; his annotations appear in several places in Peterhouse MS 95. Marchall gave several scientific and medical manuscripts to Peterhouse in 1472; the list of Marchall's donations is now preserved with the general inventory of books belonging to the College in a document known as the Roger Marchall (c. 1417-1477) Rogerus Marshall -1477 Registrum vetus ('The Old Register'). The record of Marchall's donations is in his own hand and is on a separate leaf sewn into the Registrum vetus. Marchall's donation document has the heading Billa magistri Roberti Marchall de dono suo scripta propria manu suo anno domini Millesimo 1472 and is printed as UC48.385-396 in CMBLC 10. Marchall's donation document names or describes 12 books, none of them a good match for Peterhouse MS 95; three of Marchall's donations still belong to the College, but others now belong to other institutions or have been lost. Even though Peterhouse MS 95 is not one of the books included in Marchall's donation list, Marchall owned a substantial number of scientific and medical manuscripts and could have chosen to give the volume to Peterhouse at another time rather than as a part of the 1472 gift. The Corpus of British Medieval Library Catalogues suggests that Peterhouse MS 95 may have been left to the College as part of a bequest by Master of the College, Thomas Deynman, c. 1501. Like Marchall, was also a doctor and royal physician (in Deynman's case he seems to be associated with Kings Edward IV, Henry VII and Lady Margaret Beaufort), and was a Fellow of Peterhouse before becoming its Master for a shortlived tenure c. 1500-1501. Deynman added ownership inscriptions in several places in the volume, but whether he gave the book having obtained it personally from Marchall, or whether it was simply in the Peterhouse Library and he took it into his personal possession during his association with the College is unclear. In his will, Deynman left 20 of his better books (his 'uolumina meliora') to Peterhouse, and so it is possible that if Deynman had taken personal possession of Peterhouse MS 95 then it may have passed back into the general holdings of the College's library collection upon his death. Probably owned by former Master of Sidney Sussex (1572–1643, master 1610-1643), . It seems very likely that MS Sidney 51 was seen in the possession of Samuel Ward by Ward's friend, the author and Archbishop of Armagh, Samuel Ward Samuel Ward . In Ussher's James Ussher James Ussher An answer to a challenge made by a Iesuite in Ireland (1625), Ussher wrote (abbreviations expanded, typesetting modernised): '[i]n the libraries of my worthy friends, Sir Robert Cotton, (that noble Baronett, so renowmed for his great care in collecting and preserving all antiquities) and Dr Ward, the learned Master of Sidney Colledge in Cambridge; I met with an ancient Treatise of the Sacrament (beginning thus: Sicut ante nos quidam sapiens dixit, cujus sententiam probamus, licet nomen ignoremus.) which is the same with that in the Iesuites Colledge at Lovaine, blindely fathered upon Berengarius'. The quotation that Ussher gives, 'Sicut ante nos quidam sapiens dixit, cujus sententiam probamus, licet nomen ignoremus', matches the text of the treatise on the Eucharist in Sidney MS 51, ff. 17r-26v. The text that Ussher is referring to is the Dicta Herigeri abbatis de corpore et sanguine Domini now usually attributed to , but which was for a long time believed to be by Berengar of Tours. The Heriger of Lobbes Heriger of Lobbes Dicta Herigeri survives in very few manuscript copies and the likelihood is that the one Ussher saw in Ward's hands is the same manuscript that came into the possession of Ward's former college. J. Ussher, An answer to a challenge made by a Jesuite in Ireland (1625), pp. 17-18

overview: history: Unidentified pressmark at the top of folio i recto, 'F. 6.' in ink at the top of the leaf above the medical recipe and next to the word 'Amularius'. The pressmark conforms to the Bury St Edmunds pressmark format (and that of several other religious houses), i.e., a majuscule letter followed by a Hindu-Arabic number), but the mark in CCCC MS 416 probably postdates the Bury St Edmunds pressmarking campaign by at least a century, nor is it a palaeographical match for any other Bury St Edmunds pressmarks. Further rejection of the 'F. 6.' as a Bury St Edmunds pressmark can be based on the use of an 'F' class at Bury St Edmunds being almost entirely unattested, and the Bury St Edmunds letter classes having a thematic link to the volume by either author or subject, and the letter 'F' not having an obvious relationship to the content of CCCC MS 416.

, Freeman of Norwich in 1563, alderman from c. 1570 onwards, Sheriff of Norwich in 1572-3, and Mayor of Norwich in 1587-9: his name (Francis Rugge (1536-1607) Rugge, Francis, 1536-1607ffrauncis Rugge) inscribed on p. 286. While Harvey suggests that his name is written in the hand of that of Henry Aldrich (whose name occurs twice on the same page together with scribles), it is also possible that it was added by Rugge himself, either as an owner or user of the manuscript. Although Harvey does not identify Thomas Rugge, he almost certainly is the freeman, alderman, sheriff, and mayor of Norwhich who married Anne Aldrich (d. 1611). The latter was a daughter of John Aldrich (1520-1582), alderman and mercer of Norwich, and mayor of that city in 1570-71, and Elizabeth, daughter of Nicholas Sotherton (d.1540), alderman and Mayor of Norwich (1539-40), and sister of Henry Aldrich [see below] whose name is twice inscribed above that of Francis Rugge on p. 286.

overview: history: It is probable that this bifolium (and perhaps other Parts of the volume) were a later addition to the codex. There is a 'Caucio' inscription on f. i verso dated 1330, so presumably the opening flyleaves and at least the first substantial Part of this volume (i.e., Part 2) were together at that date. These endleaves (ff. 192r-[193] verso) include a copy of a letter dated to 1400 and several nearly-illegible annotations with 15th century dates, so it is likely that these endleaves and perhaps some of the other Parts were added to the 1330 form of the volume after 1400.

It has not been established with absolute certainty when or by what means Sidney Sussex College acquired MS 51, although a plausible argument can be made that the volume was an unrecorded donation by former master . A list of Ward's donations is preserved in the college archives, but it does not appear to describe a manuscript identifiable as Sidney Sussex MS 51. It may be that Ward gave the manuscript as a separate donation, or that left Ward's possession and came to Sidney Sussex indirectly by some other route, as happened with many of Ward's personal papers (see Todd, 1985). The manuscript had certainly arrived at the College by c. 1697, when its presence was recorded in Bernard's Samuel Ward Samuel Ward Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (c. 1697), p. 104, no. 714. For an account of the early history of the library of Sidney Sussex College, see Rogers, 'Early History of Sidney Sussex College Library', esp. n. 53; Rogers points out that MS 51 is likely to have been given by Ward on the strength of MS 51's prior ownership by John Pilkington, who had also owned known Ward donation MS 55. N. Rogers, 'The Early History of Sidney Sussex College Library', in D. E. D. Beales and H. B. Nisbet (eds.), Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge: Historical Essays in Commemoration of the Quartercentenary (Woodbridge, 1996), pp. 75-88

overview: history: An inscription on f. 175r indicates that the leaf was part of a volume owned by Lanercost Priory in Cumbria, England, by 1354 at the latest: Liber ffratris Nicholai de Morland ex dono Willelmi de Langedale cuius usum proprium idem Nicholaus concessit (The book of Nicholas of Morland from the gift of William of Langdale, the use of which the same Nicholas had granted to master John of Bewcastle). The inscription names three men (Nicholas of Morland and John of Bewcastle who were granted the use of a book by William de Langdale), and of the three, only John of Bewcastle can be supplied with further biographic information as he was Prior of Lanercost (1338-1354). As Pam Robinson points out, Bewcastle, Morland and Langdale are all Cumbrian place names and so the three men mentioned in the inscription are probably all linked by geographic ties as well as social and religious connections.cessit Domino Iohanni de Buchaster

The manuscript was owned by , Master of Trinity College (1553–1558). On John Christopherson (d. 1558) Christopherson, John, -1558 f. [a] recto there is an ownership note, stating also that Christopherson had lent the manuscript to the Basel printers Froben and Episcopius: Est D. Ioannis Christofersoni Angli, Frobenio et Episcopio ab ipso crediti. The edition of Froben and Episcopius, printed in 1556 in Basel, is a Latin translation of Athanasius' works by Petrus Nannius (Pieter Nanninck, 1500-1557); the loan of a manuscript from Christopherson is acknowledged in the prefatory dedication ( ).Athanasii Magni Alexandrini episcopi, graviss. scriptoris, et sanctiss. martyris, Opera, in quatuor Tomos distributa: quorum tres sunt a Petro Nannio Alcmariano, ad Graecorum exemplarium fidem iam primum conversi, exceptis paucis antehac imperfectis ab eo denuo plenius et Latinius redditis: Quartus, Latina multorum interpretatione fere totus seorsum emissus, nunc in unum digestus et concinnatus [...], Basel 1556.

It is not known when precisely the manuscript entered the collection of Trinity College Library. In his will of 1556 John Christopherson bequeathed his books to the library; he died in 1558, but his will was not proved until 1563 (see Gaskell (1980), p. 47). The manuscript arrived in the Library after that date and before 1601, when the edition of Athanasius' works by Commelinus was printed (Heidelberg, 1601), in which the manuscript was used and cited as a codex collegii S. Trinitatis Cantabrigiensi, olim D. Joannis Christophorsoni (the introduction to Commelin's edition can be read also in PG 25, XLIII D l. 7-11). On f. I recto, p. 874, f. 892v and f. 893r there are stamps of Trinity College Library.

Add. 2603 used to belong to the Monastery of Dionysiou on Mount Athos: on f. 2r is a note of the monastery's ownership (κτῆμα μονῆς τοῦ κυρίου Διονυσίου). A similar note is found on f. 23v of CUL MS Ff.4.47. A further note indicating provenance at the Monastery of Dionysiou (απο του δεονισιου (sic) νουμερο 7 with the date 18 July 1739 was added on f. 459v by Antonios Triphillis, along with his seal (see above). Antonios Triphillis, who was an educated Greek of the diaspora, active in the first part of 18th century, may have been a dealer with access to Mt Athos monasteries or a collector, whose books were sold abroad. A similar inscription, by the same hand, can be found in CUL MS Nn.3.3, f. 1r (νουμερο 11) and CUL MS Nn.3.15.1, f. 2r (νουμερο 8), which also have the seal impression. overview: history: Jackson 1998, p. 95, finds Parts II and V in two entries in a list of texts that brought to Florence in 1492. This list is now preserved in Janus Lascaris (c. 1445-1535) Lascaris, Janus, 1445?-1535 , ff. 107r-111r. The scholia to Sophocles are listed on f. 107v line 3 as Hannover, Niedersächsische Landesbibliothek, MS XLII 1845 Antiquae Glosulae in quasdam tragaedias Sophoclis. Lascaris had been sent by Lorenzo de' Medici to the East to acquire Greek manuscripts for the Laurentian Library, and also printed the metrical scholia to Sophocles in 1518 (see Proietti 2018, pp. 226-227).Jackson 2006, p. 32, further speculates that Part I was also brought to Florence in the same year.

Along with the scholia to Sophocles in Part II, Part V is present on the list of the books brought to Florence in 1492 (see above). In Janus Lascaris (c. 1445-1535) Lascaris, Janus, 1445?-1535 , ff. 107r-111r the Enchiridion of Hephaestion is recorded on f. 107r line 9 as Hannover, Niedersächsische Landesbibliothek, MS XLII 1845 Expositio in ephestione demetrii, where "demetrii" stands for "de metris" (see Jackon 1998, p. 94).

Sir, this manuscript composed by Theodoro Ballamone of the Rites and Ceremonyes of the Greek church, hath some curiosityes in it, yet is not so perfect as I should have wished, however I desyre your acceptance of it, being the best that could heer be found, by your most affectionate servant Edw. overview: history: The manuscript was bought in 1596, in Messina, by a certain hieromonk Neophytos of Sinai for the price of 15 tarì, as it is written in an annotation on the left pastedown: ͵αφϙϛ΄ ἀγόρασα τὸ παρὸν ταρία ιε΄ Νεόφυτος ἱερομόναχος Σιναίτης ἐν Μεσσήνῃ τῆς Σικελίας.

The hieromonk Neophytos probably acquired the manuscript for Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai. The codex indeed was there in 1618/1619: this date is mentioned in an official note by Ioasaph written on f. 257v, below the last text: Ἡ παροῦσα βίβλος τῇ ἱερᾷ μονῇ τοῦ Σιναίου ἁγίου ὄρους κεκλήρωται· συνοχῇ ἀρᾶς, καὶ δεσμοῦ, τὸν σφετερησόμενον ἀπείργουσα, διὰ τοῦ παρόντος τῆς ἐμεῖς ταπεινότητος, διωρισθικοῦ γράμματος. ͵ζρκζ΄ ἐκ τοῦ (?) Σινᾶ ὄρους Ἰωάσαφ. (The last five words in monocondyle). The same note signed by Ioasaph in monocondyle is present in a manuscript which has remained until now in Saint Catherine's Monastery, MS , f. 246r (a transcription of the note is found in Sinai, Saint Catherine's Monastery, gr. 74 Δ. Στρατηγοπουλος, Τὸ χειρόγραφο Θεοτοκάριο τοῦ Ἱδρύματος Παπανικολάου (Κομοτηνή) καὶ ὁ κωδικογράφος Ἱερεμίας Μαγγαφούρης ο Σιναϊτης, in Byzantina Symmeikta 27 (2017), pp. 315-346: 337).

The codex was in the hands of the English merchant Edward Abbott, consul at Cairo in the 1650s (concerning him see Oates 1986, pp. 292-294 with bibliography), who donated it to , Fellow of King's College in Cambridge from 1625 to 1650. This is stated in a message from Abbott to Hobart written on Hobart, Nicholas, approximately 1605-1657 Nicholas Hobart (ca. 1605-1657) f. i verso, dated 16th July 1650 in Cairo: nº 1. Sir, this manuscript I obteyned by favor of a friend out of the publique library of the Bishopp of Mount Sinai resident heere in Grand Cayro, wharein though the Synopsis on Gallens' book of Terapephtike and his problems on the humours bee common, yet I suppose that the Physicall Treatises of Simeon Protomestraki of Antioch, of the most learned Psellius, and the problems of Alexander Aphrodisius, are more rare and usefull. You will finde it iust 100 yeares from this 16th of July 1650 since the finishing of this book by George of Constantinople. Wich accept from your most affectionate servant Edw. Abbott. Grand Cayro, this 16th July 1650.

The manuscript was donated to Cambridge University Library by Nicholas Hobart in 1655, as it is stated also in a note written on the upper part of f. i verso, Ex dono ornatissimi viri Nicolai Hobart Collegii Regalis quondam socii et huius Academiae insignis ornamenti. 1655. On the left pastedown is pasted the Cambridge University bookplate.
